A bayonet is a long, pointed blade — essentially a large knife, dagger, or spike — that is designed to be attached to the front end of a rifle, converting the firearm into a combined weapon: a gun and a spear at the same time.

Picture a soldier holding a rifle. Now imagine a sharp, stabbing blade locked onto the tip of that rifle's barrel. The soldier can now shoot from a distance and stab an enemy at close range. That blade is the bayonet.

A bayonet is a metal blade. Depending on the type, it can look like:

  • A long knife — flat, with a sharpened cutting edge on one or both sides. This is the most common modern form.
  • A narrow spike or rod — purely for thrusting and stabbing, with no cutting edge at all.
  • A short sword — longer and heavier than a knife, used in older military history.
  • A triangular blade — three-sided in cross-section, designed purely for deep stabbing wounds.

The blade is attached at the handle-end to a fitting — called a lug or socket — that clips, slides, or locks onto the barrel of the rifle. This means it can be attached and removed quickly.

To understand the bayonet fully, you need to understand the problem it solved.

In the early days of firearms — the 1600s and 1700s — soldiers used muskets (early rifles). These were extremely slow to reload. A soldier could fire perhaps one or two shots per minute. Once he fired, he was essentially defenseless with an empty gun while enemy soldiers could rush at him on horseback or on foot.

Before the bayonet, soldiers carried both a musket and a separate long spear called a pike. Half the army would shoot; the other half would hold pikes to protect the shooters during reloading. This was inefficient — it doubled the equipment and halved the firepower.

The bayonet solved this elegantly: every soldier could now be both a shooter and a spearman. When enemies got close, soldiers simply attached the bayonet and fought hand-to-hand. No separate weapon needed. No separate soldiers needed.
How It Is Used in Battle

When a soldier "fixes" a bayonet, it means they are attaching it to their rifle, ready for close combat. This is the origin of the famous military command: "Fix bayonets!" — heard before a charge directly into enemy lines.

A bayonet charge is one of the most dramatic acts in military history: a group of soldiers running forward at full speed toward enemy positions, rifles pointed outward with bayonets attached, intending to stab and fight at close quarters. These charges were a real and terrifying tactic in wars from the 1700s through World War II and even beyond.

Bayonet fighting is a form of combat that combines thrusting (stabbing forward), slashing (cutting sideways), and even using the rifle butt as a club — all while the bayonet is fixed.

The bayonet was one of the most important military inventions of the last 400 years. It completely changed how armies were organized and how battles were fought. Some key moments:

  • In Napoleonic Wars (early 1800s), bayonet charges decided the outcomes of major battles.
  • In World War I (1914–1918), bayonets were standard issue for all infantry. Trench warfare often turned into brutal close-range fighting where bayonets were used extensively.
  • In World War II (1939–1945), bayonets continued to be issued and used, especially in jungle warfare and urban combat.
  • Even in modern conflicts (Afghanistan, Iraq), soldiers have carried out bayonet charges in exceptional circumstances, and bayonets remain standard issue in many armies today.

Today's military bayonets are much more versatile than their ancestors. A modern bayonet is typically a knife bayonet — it functions both as a weapon attached to a rifle and as a standalone combat knife or utility tool when detached.

Modern versions often include:

  • A serrated edge for cutting rope or wire
  • A bottle opener or screwdriver slot
  • A wire-cutting function when the blade is pressed against the scabbard (the sheath that carries it)

So a modern soldier's bayonet doubles as a survival knife, cutting tool, and weapon all in one.
An Extended Meaning: The Bayonet Fitting

The word "bayonet" also appears in engineering and everyday technology, referring to a type of locking mechanism that works by inserting a piece and then twisting it a short distance to lock it in place — just like how many bayonets attach to a rifle barrel (insert → twist → locked).

You encounter bayonet fittings in:

  • Light bulbs — the kind you push in and twist to lock (common in the UK and India; these are called "BC" or bayonet cap bulbs)
  • Camera lenses — professional lenses attach to cameras via a bayonet mount (push on, twist, locked)
  • Medical and industrial connectors — many tubes and fittings use the same push-and-twist bayonet system

So if someone says "bayonet mount" or "bayonet fitting," they mean a connector that locks by twisting, named after its resemblance to the way a bayonet attaches to a gun.

A bayonet (noun) is:

  1. Primarily: A blade attached to the front of a rifle, turning it into a stabbing weapon for close combat. It can look like a knife, spike, or short sword. It was invented to give soldiers a melee weapon without needing to carry a separate one, and it shaped hundreds of years of military history.
  2. Extended meaning: Any locking mechanism that works by inserting and twisting, like bayonet-mount light bulbs or camera lenses.

The heart of the word is always the same idea: a sharp, pointed thing that locks securely onto something else — ready to be used with force.
